blocks.text: A 67-year-old man has been on intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics for five days for a fever. Blood cultures from day 1 were negative, his temperature settled on day 2, but nobody reviewed the prescription. He now has profuse watery diarrhoea and a positive Clostridioides difficile toxin test. Every antibiotic decision has a cost to the patient, to the ward and to the next patient who needs an antibiotic to work.

blocks.markdown:
**Antimicrobial stewardship** is the coordinated set of actions that promotes the right antimicrobial, at the right dose, by the right route, for the right duration. NICE guidance on antimicrobial stewardship and the UK **Start Smart, Then Focus** approach turn this into practice.

**Start Smart** applies at the first prescription. Do not start antibiotics without clinical evidence of bacterial infection. Take cultures and other samples before antibiotics where this does not delay treatment of a sick patient, and start urgently (ideally within one hour) in suspected sepsis. Prescribe according to the local guideline, check allergy status, and document the indication, drug, dose, route, and a **review or stop date**. Doses are taken from the BNF and local guidance and are not reproduced here.

blocks.title: Empirical versus directed therapy; spectrum
blocks.text: Empirical therapy is chosen before the organism is known, on the likely pathogens, the site of infection, local resistance and patient factors. Directed (targeted) therapy is chosen once culture and sensitivity results are known. Spectrum describes how many bacterial groups the drug covers: narrow-spectrum drugs cause less collateral damage to the normal flora and select less for resistance than broad-spectrum drugs.

rows: Urinary tract (community)
Escherichia coli, other Enterobacterales
Send urine culture before treatment; resistance varies locally
Community-acquired pneumonia
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, atypical organisms (for example Mycoplasma, Legionella)
Severity score guides route and regimen
Cellulitis
Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus
Beta-haemolytic streptococci are covered by narrow agents; MRSA is considered by risk
Intra-abdominal sepsis
Enterobacterales, anaerobes, enterococci
Source control matters as much as the antibiotic
Community bacterial meningitis
S. pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis (Listeria in the very young, older or immunosuppressed)
A time-critical emergency; follow the local emergency pathway
blocks.caption: Typical pathogens by site. Local guidelines and national guidance (NICE, BNF) define the regimen.

blocks.markdown: **Choosing empirical therapy** is a four-part reasoning step: (1) the most likely pathogens for the site and setting; (2) the local resistance pattern, from the hospital or community **antibiogram** (the cumulative proportion of isolates susceptible to each agent); (3) patient factors such as allergy, renal and hepatic function, pregnancy, previous resistant organisms (for example MRSA or ESBL-producing Enterobacterales) and recent antibiotic exposure; and (4) severity, which determines how urgent and how broad to be. Where a guideline exists, use it, because it already balances these factors against local data.

blocks.title: Reading a local antibiogram for a urinary infection
blocks.prompt: A 34-year-old man with no allergies and normal renal function has acute pyelonephritis but is haemodynamically stable. The (fictional) local antibiogram for 400 community E. coli urinary isolates shows resistance of 52% to amoxicillin, 30% to trimethoprim, 18% to co-amoxiclav, 12% to ciprofloxacin and 4% to gentamicin. Reason through the choice of empirical therapy.

steps.text: Identify the likely pathogen: E. coli is the commonest cause of upper urinary tract infection, so the antibiogram for E. coli is the relevant data.
Apply the resistance data. With 52% and 30% of isolates resistant, amoxicillin and trimethoprim would fail often as empirical therapy for a serious infection, so they are poor empirical choices here.

Apply patient and national safety factors. There is no allergy or renal impairment and no known resistant organism. Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin carry MHRA restrictions because of disabling and potentially long-lasting adverse effects, so they are reserved for when other options are unsuitable, even though only 12% of isolates are resistant.

Choose within the local guideline: pick the agent the guideline recommends that combines low resistance, suitable route and an acceptable safety profile. Send a urine culture before the first dose, and set a review at 48 to 72 hours to narrow or stop therapy. Check the BNF and local policy for dose and duration.

blocks.answer: Rule out agents with high local resistance, then select from the guideline-recommended agents with an acceptable safety profile, send cultures first, and plan a 48 to 72 hour review.

blocks.markdown: **Then Focus** is the review at 48 to 72 hours. With culture results, clinical progress and observations in hand, make one of the documented decisions in the table: stop, switch from intravenous to oral, change, continue, or arrange outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy (OPAT). Review is a decision, not a ritual: the default is to question whether antibiotics are still needed.

rows: Stop
No evidence of bacterial infection, or course complete
Cultures negative and a non-bacterial diagnosis confirmed
Switch IV to oral
Improving, able to take and absorb oral drugs, no need for IV (for example not a deep-seated infection requiring prolonged IV therapy)
Afebrile with falling inflammatory markers and eating normally
Change
Culture shows a resistant organism, or narrower agent is suitable
Isolate sensitive to a narrow-spectrum agent; de-escalate
Continue
Still unwell or a deep-seated infection needing ongoing IV therapy, with a new review date
Endocarditis or osteomyelitis according to specialist advice
OPAT
Needs prolonged IV therapy but is clinically stable for home or clinic administration
Specialist-led outpatient IV regimen
blocks.caption: Start Smart, Then Focus review options at 48 to 72 hours.

blocks.title: Day-3 review and IV-to-oral switch
blocks.prompt: A 58-year-old with community-acquired pneumonia has received intravenous antibiotics for 72 hours. He is afebrile for the past 24 hours, heart rate and respiratory rate are normalising, oxygen requirement has gone, and he is eating and drinking. Blood cultures are negative. Perform the review.

steps.text: Confirm clinical response against the IV-to-oral switch criteria used locally: improving, afebrile and haemodynamically stable, working gastrointestinal tract with oral intake, no condition requiring prolonged IV therapy, and normalising inflammatory markers. This patient meets them.

Check microbiology and choose the narrowest effective agent. Negative cultures mean no organism-directed change is available, so follow the guideline step-down for community-acquired pneumonia, preferring an agent with reliable oral absorption.
Document the decision: switch to oral today, the drug, dose and route per BNF and local guidance, and the stop date or total duration according to NICE and local guidance for pneumonia severity.
Safety-net: monitor temperature and symptoms after the switch and escalate if there is deterioration. A shorter, targeted course reduces both adverse effects and resistance.

blocks.answer: He meets the switch criteria: move to an appropriate oral agent, record the stop date, and monitor.

blocks.markdown: Surveillance makes stewardship visible. A common hospital measure is antibiotic consumption expressed in **defined daily doses (DDD)** per 1000 occupied bed-days, where the DDD is the WHO assumed average maintenance daily dose for the drug's main indication in adults. It allows comparison between wards and over time but does not show whether individual prescribing was appropriate.

**Drivers of antimicrobial resistance.** Resistance is an evolutionary process: antibiotic use creates **selection pressure**, and resistant organisms survive and multiply. Resistance arises by mutation or is acquired by **horizontal gene transfer** (plasmids). Mechanisms include enzymatic inactivation (beta-lactamases, including extended-spectrum beta-lactamases), altered targets (for example the altered penicillin-binding protein of MRSA), efflux pumps and reduced permeability. Drivers include unnecessary antibiotic use (for example for viral infections), broad-spectrum use when narrow would do, inappropriate dose or duration, poor infection prevention and control which spreads resistant organisms, agricultural and environmental use, international travel and a weak pipeline of new agents.

blocks.title: Collateral damage
blocks.text: Broad-spectrum agents disrupt the normal flora and are associated with Clostridioides difficile infection, with cephalosporins, clindamycin, fluoroquinolones and co-amoxiclav classically implicated, and with colonisation by resistant organisms. Good stewardship is also patient safety: unnecessary antibiotics expose the individual to harm for no benefit.

points: Start Smart: treat only when bacterial infection is likely, take cultures first, follow local guidelines, check allergy, and document indication, dose, route and review date.
Empirical choice combines likely pathogens, local antibiogram data, patient factors and severity; high local resistance rules out an agent for serious infection.
Then Focus: review at 48 to 72 hours and decide to stop, switch IV to oral, change, continue or arrange OPAT, using clinical response and culture results.
Antimicrobial resistance is driven by selection pressure and gene transfer; unnecessary, broad-spectrum or poorly dosed antibiotics and weak infection control accelerate it.
Doses and durations come from the BNF, NICE and local guidance; this lesson does not replace them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a core component of the 'Start Smart' phase?
questions.explanation: Start Smart means starting antibiotics only when indicated, after samples where possible, according to local guidance. Documenting the indication and a review date makes the later Focus review possible.

options.text: Switching all intravenous antibiotics to oral after 24 hours
Taking appropriate cultures before antibiotics where possible and documenting the indication and a review or stop date
Prescribing the broadest-spectrum agent available to avoid missing an organism
Waiting for culture results before treating any suspected sepsis

questions.correctOptionText: Taking appropriate cultures before antibiotics where possible and documenting the indication and a review or stop date

distractorRationale.a: Switching is part of the later review and needs clinical criteria, not a fixed 24 hours.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: samples, documentation of indication and review date are central to Start Smart.
distractorRationale.c: Unnecessarily broad therapy increases selection pressure and adverse effects.
distractorRationale.d: Suspected sepsis needs urgent treatment, ideally within an hour, with cultures taken without delaying it.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with cellulitis of the lower leg needs empirical therapy. Which pair of organisms is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Skin and soft tissue infections are usually caused by skin flora, mainly beta-haemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus. Empirical choice follows the likely pathogens for the site.

options.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae
Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus
Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae

distractorRationale.a: These are more typical of hospital-acquired Gram-negative infection.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: beta-haemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus are the usual causes of cellulitis.
distractorRationale.c: These are typical of intra-abdominal infection.
distractorRationale.d: These are common causes of community-acquired respiratory tract infection.

questions.stem: A hospital antibiogram shows 40% of Enterobacterales isolates from bloodstream infections are resistant to agent X. What is the most appropriate conclusion for empirical prescribing in serious infection?
questions.explanation: Empirical therapy must have a high probability of activity because there is no culture result yet. In serious infection, a high local resistance rate to an agent makes it a poor sole choice.

options.text: Agent X remains a reasonable sole empirical agent because 60% of isolates are susceptible
Agent X should be avoided as sole empirical therapy for serious infection, and the guideline should favour agents with lower local resistance
Agent X should be added to every regimen to cover resistance
Resistance data from blood cultures are irrelevant to empirical choice

questions.correctOptionText: Agent X should be avoided as sole empirical therapy for serious infection, and the guideline should favour agents with lower local resistance

distractorRationale.a: A 40% failure rate is unacceptable for a serious infection where inadequate initial therapy increases harm.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: with high local resistance, agent X is unreliable as sole empirical therapy and the guideline should prefer agents with better local activity.
distractorRationale.c: Adding an agent to which many isolates are resistant gives little benefit and increases exposure.
distractorRationale.d: Local antibiograms exist precisely to inform empirical decisions.

questions.stem: On day 3, a patient treated for presumed bacterial chest infection is afebrile with normal observations. Cultures are negative, and a respiratory virus has been detected, with no radiological consolidation. What is the most appropriate review decision?
questions.explanation: The Focus review asks whether antibiotics are still needed. A viral diagnosis with no consolidation and negative cultures supports stopping, which spares the patient adverse effects and reduces selection pressure.

options.text: Continue IV antibiotics for a full 7 days regardless
Change to a broader-spectrum antibiotic
Switch to an oral antibiotic and continue for 14 days
Stop the antibiotics, documenting the reasoning

questions.correctOptionText: Stop the antibiotics, documenting the reasoning

distractorRationale.a: There is no evidence of ongoing bacterial infection to justify continuing.
distractorRationale.b: Broadening is unwarranted when no bacterial infection is evident.
distractorRationale.c: Switching presumes bacterial infection still needs treatment, which the review evidence does not support.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the review should stop antibiotics when bacterial infection is no longer supported.

questions.stem: Which of the following best supports switching a patient from intravenous to oral antibiotics?
questions.explanation: Early IV-to-oral switch reduces line-related complications and hospital stay. It depends on clinical response, gastrointestinal function and the type of infection.

options.text: Persistent fever with rising inflammatory markers
Clinical improvement, normalising observations and the ability to take and absorb oral medication
A diagnosis of a deep-seated infection requiring prolonged IV therapy
Ongoing vomiting and a nil-by-mouth instruction

questions.correctOptionText: Clinical improvement, normalising observations and the ability to take and absorb oral medication

distractorRationale.a: Persistent fever and rising markers suggest inadequate response.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: improvement and a working gut with oral intake are core switch criteria.
distractorRationale.c: Deep-seated infections may need prolonged IV therapy unless specialists advise otherwise.
distractorRationale.d: The patient must be able to take and absorb oral drugs.

questions.stem: True or false: prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics when a narrow-spectrum agent would be effective increases selection pressure for antimicrobial resistance.
questions.explanation: Broad-spectrum agents affect more bacterial species and so select for resistance across more of the normal and pathogenic flora. They are also more strongly linked to Clostridioides difficile infection.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory tested 312 community E. coli urinary isolates against trimethoprim and found 78 resistant. Calculate the percentage of isolates resistant to trimethoprim.
questions.explanation: Resistance proportion is resistant isolates divided by tested isolates, so 78 divided by 312 equals 0.25. Expressed as a percentage this is 25%, which would be considered alongside the local guideline when choosing empirical therapy.

questions.stem: A medical ward supplied 3150 defined daily doses (DDD) of antibiotics during a month with 4200 occupied bed-days. Calculate antibiotic consumption in DDD per 1000 occupied bed-days.
questions.explanation: Consumption is total DDD divided by occupied bed-days, multiplied by 1000: 3150 divided by 4200 is 0.75, and multiplying by 1000 gives 750. Used over time, such figures help stewardship teams identify wards for audit.

questions.stem: Explain the main drivers of antimicrobial resistance and describe two biological mechanisms by which bacteria become resistant.
questions.explanation: A complete answer links ecology (selection pressure) to behaviour (prescribing and infection control) and to molecular mechanisms. Stewardship targets the behavioural drivers.
markingGuide: Selection pressure: antibiotic exposure kills susceptible bacteria and allows resistant ones to proliferate
Drivers: unnecessary use (for example for viral infections), broad-spectrum use, incorrect dose or duration
Poor infection prevention and control spreads resistant organisms; agricultural and environmental use; travel; limited new antibiotics
Acquisition by mutation or horizontal gene transfer (plasmids)
Two mechanisms named correctly, for example beta-lactamase production (including ESBLs), altered target (for example MRSA penicillin-binding protein), efflux pumps, or reduced permeability

questions.stem: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has a positive urine dipstick (nitrite and leucocytes) after a routine check. She is eating, alert as usual and afebrile, with no urinary symptoms, and the family request antibiotics. Discuss the stewardship approach.
questions.explanation: The stewardship principle is to treat the patient rather than the test result. Avoiding unnecessary antibiotics protects the individual and reduces resistance.
markingGuide: Dipstick positivity alone does not diagnose infection; asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in older adults
Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria usually gives no benefit and causes adverse effects and selection pressure
Assess for symptoms or signs of infection, take a full history and observations, and look for other causes if she becomes unwell
Withhold antibiotics, safety-net with clear advice on what to watch for and when to seek review, and communicate with the family
If infection is later suspected, send a urine culture before treatment, choose empirical therapy by local guidance and resistance, document indication and review date, and review at 48 to 72 hours
Link to resistance: unnecessary prescribing drives selection pressure and Clostridioides difficile risk
